evidence.claim: Capitol Reef Country promotes the drive for its passage from the Fremont River valley through the Waterpocket Fold to the eastern desert mesas.
evidence.quote: Spanning 75 miles from the lush Fremont River valley to the jagged mesas of the eastern desert, this route cuts directly through the heart of the Waterpocket Fold

evidence.claim: The Fremont also supplies year-round irrigation to Rabbit Valley and Caineville, linking the road’s ranching country and desert settlements through the same river.
evidence.quote: provides year-round irrigation for the agricultural lands of Rabbit Valley and Caineville.

evidence.claim: The route took shape in stages: the road from Sigurd to Hanksville became a state highway in Wayne County in 1910, followed by its Piute and Sevier County sections in 1912.
evidence.quote: The road from SR-11 (by 1926 US-89) at Sigurd southeast and east to Hanksville became a state highway in 1910 (Wayne County) and 1912 (Piute and Sevier Counties).

evidence.claim: The legislature assigned the number 24 in 1927; in 1935 the highway extended northeast toward Green River.
evidence.quote: The number was assigned in 1927 by the state legislature, and in 1935 it was extended northeast from Hanksville to US-6 near Green River.

evidence.claim: A 1961 realignment bypassed Capitol Reef Road between Fruita and Caineville.
evidence.quote: A realignment in 1961 bypassed Capitol Reef Road between Fruita and Caineville

evidence.claim: Traveling east from Loa and Bicknell, begin with ranch country and the marshlands of Bicknell Bottoms.
evidence.quote: Starting in the high-country "Green Belt" of Loa and Bicknell, the road follows the winding path of the Fremont River, passing through peaceful ranching communities and the unique marshlands of Bicknell Bottoms

evidence.claim: Near Torrey, meadows give way to red cliffs; inside the park, the route passes Chimney Rock, The Castle and Fruita’s orchards.
evidence.quote: As you head east toward Torrey, the landscape shifts dramatically. The soft green meadows give way to the towering red Wingate sandstone cliffs

evidence.claim: Loa’s name connects this Wayne County town to Hawaii: a Mormon missionary returning from there named it for Mauna Loa.
evidence.quote: The town was named after Mauna Loa, in Hawaii, by a Mormon missionary who had returned from that place.

evidence.claim: The county seat lies along State Route 24, and its post office has operated since 1879.
evidence.quote: Loa is a town in, and the county seat of, Wayne County, Utah, United States, along State Route 24.

evidence.claim: Giles depended on a river that eventually overwhelmed its irrigation works.
evidence.quote: The flooding in 1909–1910 was so severe that local church authorities gave up on trying to maintain a permanent dam. Unable to irrigate their crops, the residents began to leave.

evidence.claim: Burgess family members moved into Blue Valley by 1883 and built a dam and irrigation canal by 1884.
evidence.quote: By 1883, some Burgess family members had moved to the Blue Valley area, constructing a dam and irrigation canal by 1884.

evidence.claim: The settlement’s first name came from soil colored blue-gray by Bentonite clay and Mancos Shale.
evidence.quote: The settlement was known as Blue Valley for its blue-gray soil, colored by Bentonite clay and Mancos Shale.

evidence.claim: The town occupied both riverbanks, linked by a footbridge, though most residents lived on the south side.
evidence.quote: The town was built on both riverbanks, but most people lived on the south side. A footbridge connected the two halves.

evidence.claim: Renamed Giles in 1895, it grew to 200 people by 1900.

evidence.claim: By 1919 it was a ghost town; two rock buildings, foundations and old corrals remain.
evidence.quote: By 1919, Giles was a ghost town. Two rock buildings still stand at the site, and numerous foundations and old corrals show where the town once was.
